sources.locator: Learn Java; accessed 2026-07; Interfaces, Inheritance, Polymorphism, and composition guidance; atomic topic: Composition over inheritance
sources.claim: Composition gives an object owned or injected collaborators and delegates focused work, allowing reuse without claiming a subtype relationship.

canonicalExplanation.summary: **Composition** builds an object from **collaborators** it holds and **delegates** to: a ReportService **has a** Formatter, rather than **being** one. The collaborator is usually an **interface** passed into the constructor, so you can swap CSV for HTML formatting, or a fake one in tests, without touching the service. Compared with inheritance, composition exposes **only the operations you choose**, avoids fragile base-class coupling (a superclass change can break every subclass), and allows changing behaviour at run time. It's **not** copying another class's methods wholesale into a wrapper: expose the small interface callers need.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner builds CsvReport extends Report, then HtmlReport extends Report, then CsvEmailReport extends CsvReport, and a change to Report's constructor breaks all three. Adding PDF would mean yet more subclasses. A ReportService receives a Formatter interface and delegates formatting, so output policy changes independently of report identity. In this lesson you'll refactor a fragile hierarchy into composed collaborators with testable interfaces.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Constructors and invariants** (injecting required collaborators) and **Overriding and dynamic dispatch** (calls through interfaces).

sections.heading: The model: has-a collaborators behind interfaces
Not copying everything

examples.title: A ReportService with a pluggable Formatter
examples.situation: A ReportService receives a Formatter interface and delegates formatting, so output policy changes independently of report identity.
walkthrough: **A ReportService receives a Formatter interface:** it's passed to the constructor.
**So output policy changes independently of report identity:** switching CsvFormatter for BulletFormatter will need no change to ReportService.
examples.result: New formats are one small class each, and the service is easy to test.

examples.title: The fragile base class
examples.situation: Report's constructor gains a required parameter, and all three subclasses stop compiling.
walkthrough: Every subclass depended on the base's constructor and internals.
With composition, ReportService's constructor changes in one place.
Formatters don't depend on ReportService at all.
examples.result: A change in one component doesn't ripple through a hierarchy.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Composition means copying another class's methods into a wrapper and exposing all of them unchanged.
misconceptions.correction: Composition holds collaborators and delegates focused work, exposing only the operations its clients need.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "Not copying everything", what should the wrapper expose?

analogy.example: Composition is like **a camera with interchangeable lenses**: the camera body (service) stays the same while you swap lenses (formatters). Inheritance is **buying a whole new camera for every lens**, and a design change to the body means replacing them all.
usefulFor: remembering swap lenses, keep the body
limitations: Real lenses need mounts; interfaces are the mount standard.
A lens doesn't need to know which camera it's on.

steps.explanation: The ReportService receives a Formatter interface through its constructor.
It delegates formatting to the collaborator.

nearTransfer.prompt: Add an HtmlFormatter and a test using a fake Formatter that records the rows it received. Assert ReportService passes rows through unchanged.
scaffold: No real formatting in the test.

farTransfer.prompt: Refactor a three-level report hierarchy (with and without email) into ReportService(Formatter, Sender) with two formatters and two senders. Show all four combinations working without any subclass of ReportService.

remediation.explanation: When behaviour varies, ask: **could this variation be a collaborator passed in?** If yes, define a small interface and compose instead of subclassing.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The fragile base class".

recap.summary: To refactor a fragile hierarchy, identify what varies, extract it into a small interface, pass implementations into the constructor, delegate the focused work to them, expose only the operations clients need, and test with simple fake collaborators.
